name: Plato
title: The Teacher
tagline: He watched his teacher Socrates die for asking questions, then spent fifty years writing those questions down and built a school to keep asking them.

sep.label: Plato, by Richard Kraut (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)

g-republic.label: The Republic, tr. Benjamin Jowett (Project Gutenberg #1497)

principles.title: Examine your life
principles.idea: In the Apology, Plato's account of the trial of Socrates, Socrates tells the jury he will not stop asking questions, even to save his life. For Plato, looking honestly at how you live was the most important daily work.

quote.text: ...the unexamined life is not worth living...

principles.practice: Tonight, write down one thing you did today and ask: why did I do it that way? Write one honest answer.

principles.title: Know what you do not know
principles.idea: Socrates, as Plato tells it, found that people who claimed to be wise often were not. His small advantage was that he did not pretend. Plato's dialogues often end with no final answer, and that is part of the lesson.

quote.text: ...he knows nothing, and thinks that he knows; I neither know nor think that I know.

principles.practice: Pick a topic you talk about with confidence. Write three things about it you do not actually know for sure.

principles.title: Keep asking
principles.idea: In the Meno, a young man argues that you cannot search for what you do not know. Socrates answers that it is better, and braver, to keep looking. Plato built his whole life's work on this habit of honest searching.

quote.text: ...we shall be better and braver and less helpless if we think that we ought to enquire...

principles.practice: Choose one question you gave up on. Spend ten minutes looking into it again, and write down one thing you learn.

principles.title: Follow the reasons
principles.idea: Plato wrote in dialogues, where people test ideas by talking them through. He did not speak in his own voice; he let the arguments do the work. The goal was to go where good reasons lead, even if it is not where you expected.

quote.text: I really do not know as yet, but whither the argument may blow, thither we go.
quote.credit: Plato, Republic III, 394d, tr. Benjamin Jowett (1892)

principles.practice: Next time you disagree with someone, say their best reason back to them first, then give yours.

principles.title: Start with wonder
principles.idea: In the Theaetetus, a young student feels dizzy at a hard puzzle. Socrates tells him that this feeling is a good sign. Plato saw being puzzled not as failure, but as the first step of real learning.

quote.text: ...wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.

principles.practice: Notice one ordinary thing today that you cannot fully explain. Write it down as a question.

challenge.title: Examine the day
challenge.action: Before bed, write down one choice you made today and the real reason you made it.

challenge.title: What I do not know
challenge.action: Pick one topic you feel sure about. List three things about it you do not truly know.

challenge.title: Ask again
challenge.action: Return to one question you gave up on. Spend ten minutes looking for an answer.

challenge.title: Their best reason
challenge.action: In one disagreement, state the other person's best reason out loud before giving yours.

challenge.title: One wonder
challenge.action: Notice one everyday thing you cannot explain. Write it down as a question and ask someone about it.

challenge.title: A real dialogue
challenge.action: Like Plato's dialogues, have one conversation where you only ask questions and listen for ten minutes.

challenge.title: Your own rule
challenge.action: Read back your notes from the week. Write one rule for clear thinking in your own words.

reflect: What is one thing you were sure about this week that you have not really examined?
